comments.author: @jimogaruneto
comments.text:
My late grandmother, a cultural anthropologist, would have classified this as a fascinating case of “tradition inflation”—the ancient academic phenomenon where a simple household solution is repeatedly retold until it transforms into a profound cultural practice with a noble origin story.
According to her research (and probably a lifetime of watching Filipino families argue after meals), the original explanation was far less mystical. The true catalyst was not some grand ancestral philosophy—it was the universal rural Filipino struggle of figuring out who was going to wash a mountain of dishes after everyone had finished eating.
In many provinces, a family meal could be followed by an hour-long diplomatic summit known as “Ikaw na maghugas” (“You wash them”) versus “Hindi, ikaw naman” (“No, it’s your turn”). Generations of children perfected the ancient survival techniques of suddenly becoming busy, developing selective hearing, and mysteriously disappearing when the kitchen needed volunteers.
Then came the revolutionary discovery: banana leaves. A groundbreaking innovation in domestic labor reduction. No soaking, no scrubbing, no endless negotiations, and—most importantly—no opportunity for children to argue over dishwashing responsibilities.
Of course, history has a way of polishing inconvenient details. “Our ancestors found an efficient way to avoid washing dishes” doesn’t exactly inspire documentaries or cultural pride. So over time, the story was upgraded into a beautiful symbol of heritage, unity, and tradition.
Because apparently, “we were tired of doing dishes” is not considered a prestigious enough reason for civilization.
